query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of a boundary‐active element (e.g. boron) during alloy melting will lead to controlled segregation at the lamellar colony interfaces, thereby reinforcing interfacial cohesion and promoting efficient storage of geometrically necessary dislocations. This, in turn, will delay microcrack nucleation under room‐temperature tensile loading and simultaneously improve both strength and ductility relative to the unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with its conventional dual-phase lamellar (L12 + B2) microstructure as produced by standard casting or hybrid/cryogenic rolling and annealing processes.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small, optimized amount (e.g., ~0.5 at.%) of boron into the melt during alloy processing so that boron preferentially segregates to the interlamellar boundaries during solidification.
generation.conditions: Samples processed identically except for the boron addition, then subjected to room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests. Microstructural and interfacial characterizations (e.g. atom probe tomography, high-resolution TEM) will verify boundary segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interlamellar boundary cohesion mediated by boron segregation leads to sharper, lower-energy, and stronger boundaries, resulting in improved back-stress hardening and reduced propensity for microcrack initiation.
generation.mechanism: The trace boron acts as an interfacial ‘glue’ by lowering the boundary energy and increasing chemical bonding across lamellar interfaces. This limits local stress concentrations and promotes the storage of dislocations (generating beneficial back stresses) at or near the boundaries, ultimately suppressing early microcrack formation during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline alloy, the boron-doped alloy is expected to show a moderate increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths (e.g. on the order of ~10–20% improvement, though the exact magnitude is uncertain) along with higher elongation to failure. Fractography should reveal less pronounced brittle microcrack features at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.baseline: The conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies produced without the addition of boron, which exhibits high strength but limited tensile ductility due to microcrack initiation at numerous internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective only within the microstructural regime of eutectic alloys featuring lamellar colonies. Excessive boron could lead to the formation of brittle boride phases, so the concentration must remain at trace levels. The benefit is also assumed at room temperature for tensile deformation.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies (e.g. PMC6175879 discuss how interfacial segregation can enhance boundary strength, and PMC5227964 demonstrate the efficacy of interstitial additions in strengthening HEAs) inform the concept of boundary stabilization, applying controlled boron segregation specifically to eutectic lamellar colonies is new. The optimal boron concentration and any side effects on phase constitution remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one processed via the conventional route and the other with an addition of ~0.5 at.% boron. Characterize both alloys with TEM and atom probe tomography to document boundary chemistry and coherence. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to record yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation. Conduct fractography to assess microcrack initiation sites.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of interlamellar boundary composition (via APT)
High-resolution TEM images to assess boundary structure/coherency
Fracture surface analysis for microcrack density and morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit statistically significant simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline (or if the addition leads to formation of undesirable secondary brittle phases), then the hypothesis is falsified.

The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration.
